back.body: Body → RIGHT atrium → right ventricle → LUNGS (picks up oxygen) → LEFT atrium → left ventricle → BODY · Valves keep it one-way · Left ventricle is thickest because it supplies the whole body, not just next door · LEFT fails → backs up into the LUNGS · RIGHT fails → backs up into the BODY (ankles, neck veins)
back.why_it_matters: Follow one drop round the circuit and heart failure stops being a list to memorise.

back.body: The heart makes its OWN electricity — no nerve from the brain needed · SA node = natural pacemaker, fires fastest · AV node DELAYS the impulse so the atria can finish emptying · Then down through the ventricles, which contract · Lower sites take over if the one above fails, each SLOWER · A rhythm on the monitor does NOT prove a pulse
back.why_it_matters: The monitor watches the wiring. Your fingers watch the plumbing.

back.body: Cardiac output = HEART RATE x STROKE VOLUME · Stroke volume = what leaves per beat, set by PRELOAD (how full before the squeeze) and AFTERLOAD (what it pushes against) · Blood loss → preload down → stroke volume down → body raises RATE to compensate · That is why TACHYCARDIA is an early shock sign, before BP moves · Too fast = no filling time = output falls
back.why_it_matters: A normal heart rate proves nothing. It is one of two terms.

back.body: See the numbers card: output = rate x stroke volume; stroke volume is per-beat ejection; preload is filling; afterload is resistance; tachycardia is the early compensation and appears long before blood pressure changes.
back.why_it_matters: Everything in shock follows from this one equation.

back.body: The muscle gets NOTHING from blood inside the chambers · Coronary arteries are the FIRST branches off the aorta, just past the left ventricle · They fill mainly BETWEEN beats — contraction squeezes them shut · So a very fast rate cuts the heart's own supply · A blockage starves the muscle downstream = heart attack · Which vessel decides which territory
back.why_it_matters: More beats, yes — but less time between them, and that is when the heart drinks.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-01-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Both = a coronary artery not delivering enough · ANGINA: narrowed artery, demand outruns supply on exertion, RELIEVED BY REST · INFARCTION: blocked enough that muscle starves at rest and begins to DIE, not relieved by rest, lasts longer · Look for breathlessness, sweating, nausea, impending doom · You CANNOT tell them apart in the field — treat the worse case
back.why_it_matters: The change that matters in a known angina patient is that rest stopped working.

front.title: Angina vs. MI
front.summary: What separates them, and what does not

back.body: Angina is provoked by exertion and relieved by rest; infarction often starts at rest, lasts longer and does not settle. Angina has not yet damaged muscle; infarction is damaging it now. Neither can be reliably distinguished in the field.
back.why_it_matters: Deciding which it is feels like competence. Recognising you cannot is the competent move.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-01. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: WOMEN · PEOPLE WITH DIABETES · OLDER ADULTS are the groups most often cited · Instead of chest pain: shortness of breath alone, profound weakness, nausea or vomiting, back, jaw or shoulder discomfort, or just feeling unwell · Diabetic nerve damage BLUNTS the warning — silent infarction happens · High-risk group + unexplained symptoms = consider cardiac
back.why_it_matters: The classic picture is one way it arrives, not the only one.

front.title: Heart failure
front.summary: The fluid piles up behind whichever side failed

back.body: LEFT fails → backs into the LUNGS → breathlessness, crackles · RIGHT fails → backs into the BODY → swollen ankles, distended neck veins · Most chronic patients have BOTH · Cannot lie flat — ask about PILLOWS and whether that has changed · Acutely: sit them up, oxygen if indicated, CPAP per protocol
back.why_it_matters: Two pillows becoming three and then an armchair is the story of the illness, told in furniture.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-03. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Left-sided failure backs blood into the lungs, producing breathlessness, crackles and pink frothy sputum, and the patient cannot lie flat. Right-sided failure backs blood into the body, producing ankle swelling and distended neck veins. In chronic disease both are usually present.
back.why_it_matters: Whatever sits immediately behind the failing chamber is where the fluid goes.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-03. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Shock from the HEART failing as a pump, usually after a large MI · Volume is ADEQUATE — the pump cannot move it · Usual shock picture PLUS cardiac evidence: chest pain, breathlessness, crackles · NECK VEINS DISTENDED, not flat — that is the discriminator · FLUID IS WRONG here and floods congested lungs · Oxygen, position, fast transport, early ALS
back.why_it_matters: Empty tank, flat veins. Failed pump, full veins. That one look changes the treatment.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Defined by EVIDENCE OF ORGAN DAMAGE, not by how big the reading is · Many people live with high readings and are not emergencies · Warning features: worst-ever headache, visual disturbance, chest pain, breathlessness, altered mental status, seizure, one-sided weakness · DO NOT try to lower it in the field · Calm, position of comfort, oxygen if indicated, transport · Report the NUMBER AND THE FINDINGS together
back.why_it_matters: There is nothing to do about the reading. The question is what the reading is doing to the organs.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-05. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Aneurysm = weakened ballooning wall · Dissection = tear letting blood BETWEEN the layers · Pain: SUDDEN, severe, TEARING or RIPPING, chest through to the back between the shoulder blades, often the worst of their life with an exact known onset · Check BOTH ARMS for a blood pressure difference · Abdominal AAA: back or abdominal pain, pulsating mass — DO NOT PALPATE DEEPLY · No field treatment: recognise, gentle, fast
back.why_it_matters: Nobody describes angina as ripping. The word the patient chooses does real work here.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-06. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Unresponsive + not breathing normally + no pulse · Adults: usually a lethal RHYTHM, most often triggered by a heart attack · Children: far more often RESPIRATORY in origin · Other causes: respiratory failure, blood loss, electrolytes, drowning, electrocution, overdose, hypothermia · AGONAL GASPS look like breathing and are not · Outcome is set by early recognition, early compressions, early defibrillation — not by finding the cause
back.why_it_matters: Almost all the delay between arrest and compressions is somebody watching agonal gasps and wondering.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-02-07. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Patient's OWN prescription, per protocol, usually with medical direction · Six rights every time · ASPIRIN: reduces clot formation, CHEWED not swallowed so it works sooner; withhold for allergy and per protocol for active bleeding · NITROGLYCERIN: dilates vessels, reduces workload; BLOOD PRESSURE BEFORE AND AFTER EVERY DOSE, withhold below 90 mmHg systolic or per protocol · NOT with a head injury · MAX 3 doses per protocol · ASK EVERY PATIENT about erectile dysfunction medication in the last 24–48 h — privately — the combination can be fatal
back.why_it_matters: Seventy-two years old with his daughter in the house is exactly the patient nobody asks.

Every one is a protocol-set number and local protocol overrides.

front.title: Assisting with nitroglycerin
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: protocol or medical direction, confirm it is this patient's prescription and in date, rule out head injury, ASK about erectile dysfunction medication in the last 24–48 h privately, blood pressure before AND after (withhold below 90 mmHg systolic or per protocol), six rights, stop at three doses, reassess and document.
back.why_it_matters: Skipping the awkward question and skipping the pre-dose pressure are the two fails that hurt patients.

back.body: Minimum systolic to assist: 90 mmHg (or your protocol's higher floor) · Erectile dysfunction medication window: 24 to 48 hours depending on the drug — anything inside it is a contraindication · Head injury: contraindicated · Maximum assisted doses: 3, per protocol · Blood pressures per dose: 2, one before and one after
back.why_it_matters: These are the figures a protocol sets and an exam asks for. Confirm yours before you need them.

front.title: Chain of survival
front.summary: A chain, not a single intervention

back.body: Recognition and call for help · Early high-quality CPR · Early defibrillation · Advanced care · Post-arrest care · Recovery · Compressions rarely RESTART a heart — they keep it WORTH SHOCKING · The first two links belong to BYSTANDERS and matter more to survival than anything added later
back.why_it_matters: A patient who got compressions from a stranger in a minute has a different outcome from one who waited eight for you.

front.title: Adult CPR
front.summary: Push hard, push fast, let it come back up

back.body: Unresponsive + not breathing normally + no pulse → START · Lower half of the sternum · RATE 100 to 120/min · DEPTH at least 2 in (5 cm), no more than 2.4 in (6 cm) · FULL RECOIL — leaning stops the heart refilling · RATIO 30:2, one or two rescuers · Interruptions UNDER 10 SECONDS · SWAP compressor every 2 min · With an advanced airway: continuous compressions, 1 breath every 6 s
back.why_it_matters: Recoil is the one people get wrong without knowing it. Leaning feels like commitment and is not.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-02. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: See the numbers card: rate 100 to 120/min; depth at least 5 cm and no more than 6 cm; ratio 30:2; interruptions under 10 seconds; swap compressor every 2 minutes; with an advanced airway, continuous compressions and 1 breath every 6 seconds.
back.why_it_matters: Every one of these is revised between guideline editions — confirm against the edition your course uses.

front.title: Adult CPR
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: confirm the three findings, rate, depth, FULL RECOIL, 30:2, interruptions under 10 seconds, AED on as soon as it arrives.
back.why_it_matters: Agonal gasps are not breathing, and leaning is not compressing.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-02. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Infant = under 1 year · Child = 1 year to puberty · RATE unchanged at 100 to 120 · Child depth about 2 in (5 cm); infant about 1.5 in (4 cm) — or at least ONE THIRD of chest depth · Child: one or two hands · Infant: two fingers, or two thumbs encircling with two rescuers · RATIO 30:2 alone, 15:2 WITH TWO RESCUERS · Infant pulse: BRACHIAL
back.why_it_matters: Children arrest from breathing, not from the heart. The ratio change is that fact written down.

front.title: Paediatric CPR numbers
front.summary: What changes and what does not

back.body: See the numbers card: rate unchanged at 100 to 120; child depth about 5 cm, infant about 4 cm, or one third of chest depth; 30:2 single rescuer, 15:2 two rescuers; infant pulse at the brachial artery.
back.why_it_matters: 15:2 is the single most commonly missed number in paediatric resuscitation.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-03. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: A child is one year to puberty, compressed about 5 cm with one or two hands, pulse checked at the carotid or femoral. An infant is under one year, compressed about 4 cm with two fingers or two encircling thumbs, pulse checked at the brachial artery. Both run at 100 to 120 per minute, 30:2 alone and 15:2 with two rescuers.
back.why_it_matters: Everything except the rate and the single-rescuer ratio changes between them.

front.title: Using an AED
front.summary: On fast, everyone off, straight back on

back.body: Apply AS SOON AS IT ARRIVES — do not finish the cycle · Turn on, follow prompts · BARE AND DRY the chest; remove a medication patch under a pad · Adult pads: upper right chest, lower left side · Under 8: paediatric pads or setting IF AVAILABLE — if not, USE ADULT PADS rather than withhold the shock · CLEAR: say it AND LOOK · After the shock, RESUME COMPRESSIONS IMMEDIATELY, no pulse check
back.why_it_matters: Announcing clear without looking is how a family member gets shocked.

front.title: AED operation
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: apply as soon as it arrives, bare and dry the chest, correct pad placement, clear visually for analysis and shock, and resume compressions immediately after the shock.
back.why_it_matters: The two fails are a delayed pad and a pause after the shock.

front.title: High-performance CPR
front.summary: A pit crew, not a scrum

back.body: Roles assigned BEFORE the call: compressor, ventilator, defib operator, airway, leader · COMPRESSION FRACTION — the proportion of time compressions are actually happening — is the metric that matters · Pressure falls within seconds of stopping and takes several compressions to rebuild · Changeovers rehearsed, next compressor already kneeling · The LEADER keeps hands off the patient
back.why_it_matters: A pit crew does not decide who changes the tyre when the car pulls in.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-05. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Automated compressions at a set rate and depth · Advantage is CONSISTENCY — quality does not decay · Most valuable on stairs, in a moving ambulance, and in prolonged resuscitation · RISK: application must not create a long pause — fit it during a planned pause · Awareness level for EMTs; governed by protocol and training · Replaces compressions ONLY — everything else continues
back.why_it_matters: A person is excellent for two minutes. That is the whole argument.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-06. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Signs: palpable pulse · sudden sustained RISE in end-tidal CO2 (often first) · movement · sometimes breathing · Go straight back to AIRWAY, BREATHING, CIRCULATION and support what is failing · DO NOT HYPERVENTILATE — it raises chest pressure and starves a heart that has just restarted · RE-ARREST IS COMMON: pads stay on, team stays put · Handle gently, monitor, transport
back.why_it_matters: The moment the pulse returns, relief floods the room and discipline drops — which is exactly when they re-arrest.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-07. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: DO NOT START for: a VALID DNR or advance directive, or OBVIOUS irreversible death (decapitation, decomposition, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, injuries incompatible with life) · Otherwise START · Paperwork missing or unclear? START while somebody else finds it · Do NOT search the house yourself · STOPPING once begun is a physician or protocol decision, not yours alone · Family distress does not change the decision; your words change everything about how it lands
back.why_it_matters: Certainty from a relative is not documentation. If in doubt, your hands go on the chest.

front.title: Special situations
front.summary: Each adds one thing; none replaces the basics

back.body: DROWNING: hypoxic arrest — ventilation matters more, rescue breaths early · HYPOTHERMIA: irritable heart, handle gently, check pulse LONGER, not dead until WARM and dead · LATE PREGNANCY: manually displace the uterus to the patient's LEFT · TRAUMA: control catastrophic bleeding — compressions circulate an empty container · ELECTROCUTION: isolate the source before you approach · OVERDOSE: naloxone does not replace compressions
back.why_it_matters: The risk is hunting for the special part and forgetting the ordinary part.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-03-09. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Shock = inadequate PERFUSION — cells not getting oxygen · NOT the same as low blood pressure · COMPENSATED: fast pulse, cool pale clammy skin, anxious and restless, pressure STILL NORMAL — the body is winning · DECOMPENSATED: pressure falls, mental status changes, pulse thready — the body has lost · IRREVERSIBLE: damage persists even if perfusion returns · Catch it in the COMPENSATED stage
back.why_it_matters: The early signs are the body fighting. The late signs are the body losing.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-01. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

front.title: Compensated vs. decompensated
front.summary: Where you want to catch it

back.body: Compensated shock holds a normal blood pressure with a fast pulse, cool pale clammy skin and an anxious restless patient — the compensation is working. Decompensated shock has a falling pressure, a thready or slowing pulse, cold mottled skin and a confused or drowsy patient. The first is where intervention still works.
back.why_it_matters: Waiting for the pressure to drop means waiting until the body has already been overrun.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-01. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Loss of circulating volume, usually blood · HIDDEN bleeding: chest, abdomen, pelvis, THIGHS — two broken femurs alone can do it · Also vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, heat illness · Fast weak pulse, cool pale clammy skin, thirst, anxiety, FLAT NECK VEINS · Control bleeding, oxygen, KEEP WARM, position per protocol, MOVE — the fix is surgical
back.why_it_matters: A patient can bleed to death internally while looking, at first glance, largely intact.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-02. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: The pump has failed; volume is ADEQUATE · Usually a large MI, also arrhythmias and end-stage heart failure · NECK VEINS DISTENDED and lungs often WET · FLUID IS WRONG — it floods congested lungs · Position follows the breathing: usually UPRIGHT, not flat · Can present without chest pain · Recognition, oxygen, position, short scene time, early ALS
back.why_it_matters: Same shocked patient, opposite neck. That look decides whether fluid is medicine or poison.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-03. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Vessels dilate — same volume, bigger space · SEPTIC: overwhelming infection, may be WARM and FLUSHED early · ANAPHYLACTIC: fast, with airway swelling, wheeze, hives, gut symptoms — the one with a time-critical specific treatment, assisted per protocol · NEUROGENIC: spinal cord injury, vessels below lose their signal → WARM, DRY, PINK skin and a pulse that is NOT FAST
back.why_it_matters: A shocked patient who is not tachycardic should make you think neurogenic.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Most shock gives cool, pale, clammy skin and a fast pulse. Neurogenic shock gives warm, dry, pink skin below the injury and a pulse that is normal or slow, because the same spinal injury cut the pathway that would otherwise speed the heart. The patient looks well and is not.
back.why_it_matters: If you only learn one exception in shock, learn this one.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Heart works, volume adequate, something OUTSIDE is blocking flow · TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX: air compressing heart and great vessels — develops while you work · CARDIAC TAMPONADE: fluid round the heart stops it filling · MASSIVE PE: clot blocking outflow to the lungs · ALL THREE: DISTENDED NECK VEINS · Fluid does not fix any of them · Recognise, call ALS, move
back.why_it_matters: Full neck veins in a deteriorating chest trauma patient puts tension pneumothorax at the top of the list.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-05. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: MENTAL STATUS: anxious and restless early, confused and drowsy late · SKIN: cool, pale, clammy (exception: neurogenic) · PULSE: fast and weakening (exception: neurogenic) · NECK VEINS: FLAT = volume loss, fluid helps · DISTENDED = pump failure or obstruction, fluid harms · BLOOD PRESSURE CHANGES LAST — never the trigger · Children hold pressure even longer
back.why_it_matters: The neck is the observation most often skipped and the one that sorts the categories.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-06. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: See the numbers card: mental status early then late; skin cool pale clammy with the neurogenic exception; pulse fast and weakening with the same exception; FLAT neck veins mean volume loss and fluid helps; DISTENDED neck veins mean pump failure or obstruction and fluid harms; blood pressure changes last.
back.why_it_matters: Two seconds at the neck changes the treatment.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-04-04-06. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: RECOGNISE from skin, pulse and mental status — not from a cuff · CONTROL external bleeding first · Airway, breathing, oxygen as indicated · KEEP THEM WARM — cold impairs clotting; blankets are TREATMENT · Position per protocol, but BREATHING OVERRIDES if the lungs are congested · NOTHING BY MOUTH — they may go to surgery · Early ALS, short scene time · REASSESS: shock moves
back.why_it_matters: Almost nothing that fixes shock happens in the back of an ambulance. Recognition, bleeding, warmth and time are what you control.

front.title: Bleeding control and shock management
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: standard precautions, control external haemorrhage, airway and breathing with oxygen, recognise shock without waiting for a blood pressure, KEEP WARM, nothing by mouth, early ALS and short scene time, reassess and document the trend.
back.why_it_matters: The neglected step is warmth, and the consequence does not show on a monitor until much later.
